But version was previously an unknown key: validate_skill() logged a warning and registered the skill anyway. Anything carrying version: 1.0, version: v2, or a date now fails registration outright. The alternative — warn and continue — was rejected. A version that may or may not be parseable cannot be used for pinning or comparison, which is the entire reason for the field; a lenient validator would ship the syntax without the guarantee.

get_metadata() needed no change. It already returns the parsed frontmatter dict verbatim, so the field surfaced the moment it became legal. The criterion was satisfied by validation alone. Worth noting for future frontmatter fields: the only real work is validation and catalog rendering.

Type errors are more likely than syntax errors, so they get the better message. A non-str value reports the actual parsed type and its repr, names YAML coercion as the cause, and shows the corrected line — version: "1.0.0". Reporting "expected str, got float" would have been technically accurate and practically useless, because the author wrote something that looks like a version and has no reason to suspect the parser. This is the same failure mode as the existing _OPTIONAL_FIELDS type loop, which is why version is validated separately rather than added to that table.

Catalog rendering is conditional. <version> and - **Version**: are emitted only when the field is set. The catalog goes into the system prompt on every turn, so unversioned skills must not pay for a feature they do not use.

validate_version() is exported. The Hub needs to validate a version at publish time, before a Skill object exists. Keeping the rule in one place is cheaper than having the Hub reimplement the regex and drift from it.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
The semver regex is inlined, and that is a deliberate maintenance liability. It is stable — semver 2.0.0 has not changed since 2013 — but if the SDK ever needs comparison (range matching, "is this newer than that") rather than validation, a regex will not do it and the semver package should be adopted then. Validation alone does not justify the dependency.

_KNOWN_KEYS and _OPTIONAL_FIELDS are now out of step. _KNOWN_KEYS is derived from _OPTIONAL_FIELDS plus a literal set that now carries version. A third specially-validated field will make this genuinely confusing. When that happens the field table should become {name: validator} rather than {name: type}, which would fold the required fields, the optional type checks, and version into one declaration.

docs.title: 7. Distinguish "not found" from "unavailable" in the HTTP provider
docs.text:
Labels: theme:resilience, type:bug, theme:security, package:core, package:http

Status: implemented. Scope grew to include agentskills-core (the new SkillUnavailableError) and a credential leak confirmed during the work.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: HTTPStaticFileSkillProvider maps every non-2xx response — and every transport failure — to SkillNotFoundError. A 503, a DNS failure, and a genuine 404 are indistinguishable to the caller, so nobody can implement sensible retry or alerting. A transient blip currently looks like a missing skill.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
• New SkillUnavailableError(AgentSkillsError) in core for transient/transport failures.
  • 404/410 → SkillNotFoundError. 5xx, 429, timeouts, connection errors → SkillUnavailableError.
  • 401/403 get a distinct message that does not echo credentials.
  • Bounded retry with exponential backoff and jitter for retryable classes only; honour Retry-After. Retry count and timeout configurable on the constructor.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Error taxonomy implemented and documented in the package README error table
  • [x] Retries only on retryable classes, with a cap
  • [x] Retry-After honoured
  • [x] No credential material in any exception message
  • [x] Tests per status class via respx

docs.title: Pre-implementation notes
docs.text:
The "no credential material" criterion is already violated today, via exception chaining. The provider raises AgentSkillsError(...) from exc, and the chained httpx exception's repr contains the full request URL — including the query string. Any deployment passing a SAS token or signed-URL credential through params leaks it into every traceback and every log line that renders one. Sanitising only the message we construct is not sufficient; the cause has to be suppressed or the URL redacted before chaining. This is a live issue, not a future one, and it is the reason this item should be treated as security-relevant rather than purely ergonomic.

Retry must not swallow 304. _stream_bytes returns (None, headers) on a conditional-request hit. A retry wrapper that treats "no body" as a failure would break revalidation, and 304 must not be classified as unavailable.

Retries interact with the manifest path. A missing index.json is an expected 404 that is translated to ResourceListingNotSupportedError; it must stay on the non-retryable branch.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
The credential leak was real and is fixed. Confirmed: raise_for_status() produces an httpx.HTTPStatusError whose message embeds the full URL, query string included, and chaining it put that into every rendered traceback. The cause is now suppressed with from None throughout the request path. Two regression tests assert on traceback.format_exception(...) output rather than on str(exc) — testing only the message would not have caught the original bug, since the message was already clean.

Messages carry a base-relative path, not a redacted absolute URL. The first attempt redacted the query string and kept scheme and host, which is the conventional fix. It was abandoned because an existing security test asserts the base URL never appears in a message at all, and that guarantee is worth keeping: the host is the one piece an operator can always recover from configuration, whereas a leaked path in a shared log is not recoverable. Errors now read HTTP 503 from /incident-response/SKILL.md, which is enough to debug.

401/403 are AgentSkillsError, not SkillUnavailableError. Retrying a rejected credential is pointless and, against hosts with lockout policies, harmful. They get a message naming headers/params as the thing to check, without echoing either.

A Retry-After beyond max_retry_delay fails immediately rather than sleeping. Honouring a literal Retry-After: 3600 would park a request path for an hour. The advice is not discarded — it is attached to the exception as retry_after so a scheduler can act on it — but the decision to wait that long belongs to the caller, not to a provider.

Full jitter, not equal jitter. random.uniform(0, delay). The registry builds its catalog concurrently, so without jitter every skill fetch retries in lockstep and hits the recovering server as a single wave. The tests pin the bound by stubbing random.uniform, not the value.

304 stayed on the success path, as flagged above; the revalidation tests already covered it and continue to pass unchanged.

Observation. SkillUnavailableError.retry_after is currently only ever populated by the HTTP provider. If a second provider gains transient failures, the backoff loop itself is the next thing to lift into core — it is provider-agnostic apart from the status-code mapping.

docs.title: 8. Structured logging across the SDK
docs.text:
Labels: theme:operability, type:feature, package:core, package:fs, package:http

Status: implemented. Scope grew to agentskills-mcp-server, whose existing logger sat outside the namespace.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Outside one warning in validation.py, the SDK is silent. There is no way to see which skills were fetched, how long a fetch took, or why a provider fell back — which makes production support guesswork.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
• Module-level loggers under a consistent agentskills.* namespace.
  • Library attaches no handlers and adds NullHandler; the host application configures output.
  • DEBUG for fetch/parse/cache events, INFO for registration outcomes, WARNING for degraded behaviour.
  • A redaction helper applied to anything containing a URL, header, or query string so Authorization values and SAS tokens never reach a log record. Pairs with the error messages in issue 7.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Consistent logger namespace, NullHandler attached
  • [x] No secret material in any log record (test with a provider configured with a bearer token and a SAS-style query param)
  • [x] Logging conventions documented in docs/DEVELOPMENT.md

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
logging.getLogger(__name__) does not produce a namespace, and that was the actual bug. The two existing loggers were named agentskills_core.validation and agentskills_mcp_server.config. Those are siblings, not descendants of a common root, so logging.getLogger("agentskills").setLevel(DEBUG) reached neither. Distribution names use underscores; logger hierarchies use dots. get_logger(__name__) rewrites the prefix — agentskills_http.static → agentskills.http.static — which keeps the logger name tied to the module it lives in while giving the whole SDK one dial. Hand-written logger strings were rejected: six packages' worth of literals rot silently when a file moves.

The NullHandler is attached once to the namespace root, not per module. The standard library documents the per-module form, but that only exists because most libraries have no common root. We do.

There is no ERROR level anywhere in the SDK, deliberately. Every failure path already raises. Logging it as well reports one event twice and quietly takes the severity decision away from the caller, who is the only party who knows whether a missing skill was fatal. The one WARNING that is not a retry — an unrecognised metadata key — is a case where nothing is raised at all.

Redaction reuses issue 7's work rather than inventing a second mechanism. The HTTP provider already had a private _describe() returning a base-relative path. That is strictly stronger than the "strip the query string" helper this issue proposed, and building a second, weaker sanitiser for logs would have guaranteed drift between what an exception says and what a log line says. _describe() was lifted into core as redact_url(url, relative_to=...), now tested directly, and _describe() is a one-line call through to it.

One real bug surfaced while lifting it: the old implementation ended or url, falling back to the raw URL when the relative path came out empty — which happens when the fetched URL equals the base. That fallback leaked the query string in exactly the situation it was meant to protect. redact_url() now falls back to a host-and-path form with the query replaced, never the raw input.

Headers are not logged, redacted or otherwise. A redact_headers() helper was considered and dropped. No operational question is answered by a header value, and a redactor that only works if every future caller remembers to invoke it is a trap — the safe default is to have nothing to redact. Same reasoning drove the explicit ban on exc_info for transport failures: httpx exception reprs embed the full request URL, so _logger.warning(..., exc_info=exc) in the retry loop would have re-opened the exact leak issue 7 closed. There is a comment at that line saying so.

The retry loop is where the real value is. Before this change a provider could burn three attempts and several seconds of backoff with no external trace whatsoever. That is now a WARNING naming the sanitised path, the sleep, and the attempt number.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
agentskills_core/logging.py shadows a standard-library module name. It is safe — Python 3 absolute imports mean import logging inside the package still resolves to the stdlib — and it matches the package's existing noun-per-module convention (encoding, parsing, validation). Flagged because it reads like a bug at a glance and will attract at least one drive-by "fix".

The secret-leak tests assert on caplog.text, and one of them asserts the log is non-empty. A test that greps for a token in an empty buffer passes for the wrong reason. Worth copying to any future test of the same shape.

Timing is still not instrumented. The issue's problem statement asked how long a fetch took; nothing here answers that. Emitting durations means either wrapping every provider call in a timer or exposing metrics properly, and the second is the honest answer. Deferred to the observability work rather than half-solved with time.monotonic() deltas sprinkled through the providers.

docs.title: 9. Enforce a coverage floor in CI
docs.text:
Labels: theme:project-health, type:chore, good-first-issue

Status: implemented.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: pytest-cov is not a dev dependency and CI has no coverage gate, so regressions in test coverage are invisible.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text: Add pytest-cov, wire python scripts/dev.py test:cov into the CI test job, set a floor (start at current measured coverage, ratchet upward), publish the report, and add a badge.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Coverage measured per package and in aggregate
  • [x] CI fails below the floor
  • [x] Badge in the root README

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
The pre-existing test:cov task measured the wrong thing. It passed --cov=packages, a path, which counts the test files as covered code. A test file is trivially covered by the act of running it, so 2,822 of the 3,712 measured statements were tests marking themselves 100%. Reported coverage was 99%; real library coverage was 96.42%. Coverage is now configured with source_pkgs — import names, not paths — so only shipped code is measured. Branch coverage is on, which the old configuration also lacked.

An aggregate floor alone is not a gate, and the issue's first criterion is why. With six packages summed, agentskills-mcp-server can sit at 91% indefinitely because agentskills-core at 99% carries the average. Floors are therefore enforced at two levels: the aggregate through [tool.coverage.report] fail_under, so that even a bare coverage report is gated, and per package through COVERAGE_FLOORS in scripts/dev.py, which runs coverage report --include once per distribution against the same .coverage file. This was verified rather than assumed: adding five uncovered statements to agentskills_core fails the per-package gate at 97% against its floor of 99, while the aggregate does not move off 96%. An aggregate-only gate would have passed that change.

Floors start at the measured value, truncated to an integer — core 99, fs 97, http 96, langchain 100, agentframework 100, mcp_server 91, aggregate 96. Setting them lower "for headroom" bakes in slack that nobody ever removes. Two packages sit at 100, which means any new uncovered line fails CI; for a package that is currently fully covered that is the correct signal, not an inconvenience.

Floors live in exactly one place each. The aggregate is in pyproject.toml because coverage enforces it natively; the per-package values are in dev.py because nothing enforces those natively. The aggregate is deliberately not repeated in dev.py — the final coverage report call passes no --fail-under, so it reads the value from config. Two copies of a threshold is two thresholds.

The badge states the enforced floor, not a measurement. coverage ≥96% is guaranteed true by CI on every commit. A live per-commit percentage needs Codecov or Coveralls, which means an account, a repository authorisation, and usually a token — a decision for the maintainer, not something to slip into a chore PR. A hand-updated static number would have been the worst of both: it can silently claim 96% while the truth is 80%. The floor formulation cannot drift misleadingly, because raising the floor and updating the badge are the same commit by construction. The live number is still visible: the CI job writes the full report to the GitHub Actions job summary of every run, and uploads coverage.xml and htmlcov/ as an artifact.

Coverage runs as its own job, not inside the test matrix. Running it three times across 3.12/3.13/3.14 would triple the cost to answer the same question, and a version-dependent coverage difference would be a finding in its own right rather than something to average away.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
scripts/dev.py claimed to be "Development task runner for Pallium". Copied from a sibling repository and never corrected. Fixed in passing.

scripts/ is not in the lint scope. CI runs ruff over packages/ examples/ only, so dev.py has drifted from the formatter — ruff format wants to rewrite lines this change did not touch. Left alone rather than mixing a whole-file reformat into a coverage PR, but the scope should be widened and the file formatted once, deliberately.

The gate's floor sits just below three known soft spots, which is worth naming rather than quietly accepting. In order of value: agentskills_mcp_server/__main__.py at 75% — the documented way to launch the server, with its config-loading error paths and the entire _build/run path untested; agentskills_mcp_server/context_provider.py at 83%, where the uncovered block is the import guard added by issue 11, so the two carefully worded upgrade messages have never been executed; and the _stream_bytes size-limit branches in the HTTP provider. These are the ratchet's first targets.

Output ordering in dev.py was scrambled. Its banners are printed by Python and buffered, while subprocess output goes straight to the terminal, so every banner appeared after every command's output — unreadable in a CI log with eight sequential invocations. Fixed with an explicit flush.

docs.title: 10. Automate PyPI publishing with Trusted Publishing
docs.text:
Labels: theme:project-health, type:chore

Status: implemented. Requires one-time Trusted Publishing configuration on PyPI and TestPyPI (six projects each) plus two GitHub Environments before the first tag; see DEVELOPMENT.md. Until that is done, the workflow runs and fails at the upload step.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Releasing means a maintainer running scripts/publish.ps1 locally with PyPI credentials, in dependency order, across six packages. It is manual, unauditable, requires a long-lived token on a workstation, and is easy to get half-done.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
GitHub Actions workflow triggered by the release tag, using PyPI Trusted Publishing (OIDC, no stored token):

  • Build all six packages
  • Publish in dependency order: core → providers → integrations
  • Gate on a GitHub Environment requiring manual approval
  • Dry-run to TestPyPI on release-candidate tags
  • Attach build provenance attestations (prerequisite for artifact signing in v1.0)

Keep publish.ps1 for local/emergency use.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Tag push publishes all six packages with no stored credentials
  • [x] Dependency order enforced; a failure mid-sequence is clearly reported
  • [ ] TestPyPI path verified end-to-end — blocked on the one-time setup below. The routing, the build loop and the version guard were exercised locally; the upload itself cannot be verified until the TestPyPI trusted publishers exist. Run the workflow manually once they do, before the first real tag.
  • [x] Release process in docs/DEVELOPMENT.md updated

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
Tag routing allow-lists rather than deny-lists. The obvious reading of "dry-run to TestPyPI on release-candidate tags" is to match -rc and send those to TestPyPI. That fails open: a typo'd tag, a nightly, or a v0.3 with a missing component all match nothing and go straight to production. The condition is inverted instead — only ^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ reaches PyPI, and everything else falls through to TestPyPI. Verified against v0.3.0, v0.3.0rc1, v0.3.0-rc.1, v1.2.3, nightly and v0.3. The worst outcome of a bad tag is now a wasted TestPyPI version, not a burnt PyPI one.

One approval, not six. GitHub environment reviewers approve per job, so the natural one-job-per-package layout would have demanded five or six approvals per release. Building is therefore split from publishing: one build job produces all six distributions in parallel, and one publish job uploads them as six sequential steps behind a single environment gate. Sequential steps also satisfy "a failure mid-sequence is clearly reported" better than a matrix — the step name is the package name, and matrix ordering is not guaranteed even at max-parallel: 1.

skip-existing: true on both targets. The issue's own complaint is that a release is "easy to get half-done"; that is only true if resuming is impossible. With skip-existing, re-running the failed job finishes the release instead of erroring on the packages that already went up. The failure mode this normally introduces — silently publishing nothing because the version was never bumped — is closed by the version guard rather than by refusing to resume.

A version guard runs before anything is built. scripts/check_release_version.py reads all six pyproject.toml files, asserts they agree, and asserts the agreed version equals the tag minus its v. Exact string comparison rather than PEP 440 parsing, so the tag, the wheel filename, and the PyPI page are spelled identically; the cost is that a pre-release must be tagged v0.3.0rc1, not v0.3.0-rc.1. The script is useful on its own before tagging.

Dependency order is a user-visible property, not a PyPI constraint. PyPI will happily accept agentskills-fs before agentskills-core exists — dependencies resolve at install time. The order matters only for the window during a release when someone runs pip install. Recorded in a comment, because the natural assumption is that the ordering is technically required, and someone will otherwise "optimise" it into a parallel matrix.

Script injection was avoided in the shell steps. Tag names reach the runner as data, so github.ref_name is passed through env: and referenced as "$REF" rather than interpolated into the script body with ${{ }}.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
The GitHub Release was being created whether or not publishing worked. release.yml fired on the same tag, independently and immediately, so it would have produced a release announcing 0.3.0 even if every upload failed — and, once the approval gate existed, it would have announced the release before the reviewer approved it. The job moved into publish.yml behind needs: publish, and release.yml is deleted. Tags that route to TestPyPI now produce a GitHub pre-release rather than a full one.

Six PyPI projects × two indexes = twelve trusted-publisher configurations, none of which can be created from the repository. This is the one part of the release path that stays manual, and it fails at the last step of the first release if it is skipped. Called out at the top of this issue and in DEVELOPMENT.md rather than left to be discovered.

publish.ps1 is now emergency-only and should be labelled as such in the script itself. It is the only remaining path that needs a long-lived token, and the whole point of this change was to stop those existing. Left in place per the proposal, but it will drift.

Found while preparing 0.3.0: the inter-package constraints would have shipped issue 11 again. Every dependent required agentskills-core = ">=0.1.0,<1.0", and agentskills-mcp-server had no upper bound at all. But agentskills_mcp_server/config.py imports get_logger, which this milestone added — so pip install agentskills-mcp-server==0.3.0 could legally resolve core 0.1.0 and fail at import, exactly as the published 0.2.3 packages did. Floors raised to >=0.3.0,<1.0; check_release_version.py now refuses to build unless every dependent requires the core version being released, and bump-version.ps1/.sh rewrite the constraint alongside the version so it cannot drift again. The six ship in lockstep, so exact-match is the right rule.

docs.title: 11. Restore compatibility with Agent Framework 1.x
docs.text:
Labels: theme:correctness, type:bug, package:agentframework, package:mcp-server

Status: implemented.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
agent-framework-core renamed BaseContextProvider to ContextProvider. Both integrations still import the old name:

from agent_framework import BaseContextProvider, FunctionTool

Our constraint is agent-framework-core = ">=1.0.0rc3,<2.0", which admits 1.12.1, so a fresh pip install agentskills-agentframework resolves the new version and raises ImportError at import time. The published 0.2.3 packages are broken for anyone installing today. CI and local runs pass only because poetry.lock pins 1.0.0rc3.

Confirmed on a clean Python 3.14 environment: 23 failures across agentskills-mcp-server/tests/test_context_provider.py, plus collection errors in both agentskills-agentframework test modules. Every one traces to this rename.

A second defect compounds it. The lazy import in context_provider.py catches ImportError and re-raises:

AgentSkillsMcpContextProvider requires agent-framework. Install it with: pip install agentskills-mcp-server[agentframework]

The package is installed. The advice is wrong, and it sends the user to reinstall a dependency they already have instead of revealing the version incompatibility.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
• Import ContextProvider, falling back to BaseContextProvider so both generations work, or drop the fallback and raise the floor to the release that introduced the new name.
  • Decide the supported range deliberately and encode it. <2.0 was never verified against anything past the release candidate.
  • Re-raise the original exception as __cause__ so the real error survives, and only claim the dependency is missing when it genuinely is.
  • Add a CI job that resolves dependencies without the lock file, so upstream breaking changes surface here rather than in a user's install.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Both integrations import cleanly against agent-framework-core 1.12.1
  • [x] Full suite passes on a lock-free install
  • [x] Version constraint reflects the range actually tested
  • [x] The "requires agent-framework" message appears only when the package is absent
  • [x] Unlocked-resolution job added to CI

docs.title: Open question
docs.text: allow-prereleases and its TODO: Remove once a stable 1.0+ is available are now obsolete — 1.12.1 is stable. Removing the flag belongs with this fix.

docs.title: 12. Support Python 3.14
docs.text:
Labels: theme:project-health, type:bug, package:all

Status: merged, awaiting release.

Every package pinned python = ">=3.12,<3.14", so installation failed outright on current stable Python. The README attributed this to upstream dependencies; none of them justified it. pyyaml, httpx, langchain-core, mcp, pydantic, pyjwt and agent-framework-core all declare 3.14 support. The cap was inherited across all six packages, including agentskills-core, whose only dependency is pyyaml.

Ceiling raised to <4.0 rather than removed, because langchain-core declares <4.0.0 and Poetry requires a project range that is a subset of its dependencies. 3.14 added to the CI matrix and the classifiers.

Verified on Python 3.14.6: all six packages install, and 265 tests pass. The only failures are issue 11 above, which is unrelated to the Python version.

The fix has no effect until a release goes out — the <3.14 cap is baked into the 0.2.3 metadata already on PyPI and cannot be changed retroactively.

docs.title: Unblocked side note
docs.text: mypy is referenced by scripts/dev.py and docs/DEVELOPMENT.md but is not installed in the dev environment, so dev.py typecheck and dev.py check fail. Worth folding into issue 9 or filing as a separate type:chore.

docs.title: v0.4 "Developer Experience"
docs.text:
Specifications for the v0.4 roadmap items, in the same order as the table in the roadmap. Milestone: v0.4.

Add the GitHub issue number to a heading once the item is filed.

docs.title: 1. agentskills CLI
docs.text:
Labels: theme:dx, type:feature, package:cli

Status: implemented. Both open questions were resolved toward the dependency-light answer; see the implementation notes.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: There is no way to work with a skill without writing Python. Validation only happens inside registry.register(), at runtime, in someone's application — so a malformed SKILL.md is discovered by an agent failing to start rather than by the author who wrote it. Authoring a new skill means copying an existing folder and hoping the frontmatter is right.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
A new agentskills-tools package exposing an agentskills entry point.

Command Behaviour agentskills init <name> Scaffold SKILL.md with valid frontmatter plus empty references/, scripts/, assets/ folders. agentskills validate <path> Run validate_skill() against one skill or a directory of them. Human-readable output by default, --format json for machines. Exit non-zero on failure — this is the contract CI depends on. agentskills lint <path> Non-fatal quality warnings: description too long for a catalog, body over a token budget, resources present but never referenced from the body, missing version. agentskills inspect <path> Render what an agent would actually see — the catalog entry, the metadata, the body — so authors can check token cost before shipping. agentskills serve <path> Run the MCP server over a folder of skills without hand-writing a server.json.

Keep the dependency footprint small; the CLI should install without pulling in any framework integration.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Separate package, or an extra on agentskills-core (pip install agentskills-core[cli])? A separate package keeps core dependency-light, which is a stated product principle.
  • Which argument parser — stdlib argparse (no dependency) or typer/click (nicer UX, extra dependency)?

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] All five commands implemented with --help
  • [x] validate exits non-zero on any failure and zero on success
  • [x] validate handles both a single skill folder and a directory of skills
  • [x] --format json output is stable and documented
  • [x] Installs without any framework integration dependency
  • [x] Package README with examples

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
Both open questions were answered the same way, for the same reason. A separate agentskills-tools package rather than agentskills-core[cli], and stdlib argparse rather than click or typer. Item 2 installs this CLI into other people's CI, so every dependency it carries is a supply-chain edge those repositories inherit for the privilege of checking a markdown file. argparse costs some polish in --help; that is the whole price.

The MCP server is an optional serve extra for the same reason: mcp and pydantic have no business being installed by a job that only runs validate.

The forgiving parser was the actual problem worth solving. split_frontmatter() returns ({}, raw) on a YAML error rather than raising — a deliberate choice in core, since a provider should not explode on one bad skill. But it means a mistyped colon arrives at validate_skill() as "metadata missing required 'name'" and "metadata missing required 'description'", which tells an author nothing about what is wrong. The CLI therefore parses the frontmatter itself first and reports the real cause: missing delimiter, unclosed block, oversized block, invalid YAML, or a sequence where a mapping belongs. Spec checks are skipped when that fails, because they can only restate the damage.

This is also where line numbers come from. problem_mark.line + 1 maps a YAML error back to a SKILL.md line, which is exactly what item 2 needs to annotate a pull request diff inline — without it the Action can only annotate at file level.

Exit code 2 exists to keep "found a problem" apart from "could not look". A missing path, an uninstalled extra, and an unwritable directory all exit 2; broken skills exit 1. A workflow that collapses every non-zero into "invalid skill" reports a typo in a path as a spec violation, and the author goes looking for a fault in a file that is fine.

The scaffold is validated before it is written. init builds an in-memory provider over the template and runs the real validate_skill() against it. That rejects init "Bad Name" without copying _NAME_RE into this package, and it means the template we ship cannot quietly drift out of conformance — if the spec tightens, init starts failing its own output.

Lint thresholds are opinions, so they are named and adjustable. --max-body-tokens is a flag; the 500-character catalog description ceiling is a constant with the reasoning attached (a catalog entry is charged on every turn, a body only when loaded). Token counts are len(text) / 4, which is honest enough to flag an outlier and nowhere near a real tokenizer.

docs.title: Observations for later
docs.text:
lint cannot warn about unknown frontmatter keys. Core recognises exactly seven, warns about anything else at registration, and keeps that set in a private _KNOWN_KEYS. Surfacing it here would mean duplicating the constant in a second package — the drift trap already on the follow-ups list. Core should export the known-key set; until it does, this lint is absent rather than wrong.

A seventh package must be registered in seven places — root pyproject.toml three times (path dependency, source_pkgs, isort first-party), COVERAGE_FLOORS, both bump scripts, check_release_version.py, and publish.yml twice (build loop and publish step). Only the last one fails silently: everything else errors, but a package missing from publish.yml simply never ships. Recorded in .github/copilot-instructions.md.

agentskills-tools is a new PyPI project, so it needs a pending trusted publisher registered before the v0.4.0 tag — and the pending-publisher uniqueness limit documented in item 12 means it cannot be registered alongside another pending one.

The distribution is named agentskills-tools, not agentskills-cli. PyPI rejected the latter: its name-similarity check ultranormalizes a name (lowercase, strip -/_/., map l/i to 1 and o to 0) before comparing, and the unrelated agent-skills-cli project already collides under that rule. The rename landed after the v0.4.0 tag had already published seven of the nine distributions, so the tag was recreated on the fix commit and the already-live packages were skipped on re-upload. Any new distribution name must be checked against https://pypi.org/pypi/<name>/json (404 means free) and against its hyphenated variants before a pending publisher is registered.

docs.title: 2. Skill validation GitHub Action
docs.text:
Labels: theme:dx, type:feature

Depends on: item 1 (CLI)

Status: implemented. Annotations are emitted by the CLI itself as --format github, so the action stays a composite wrapper with no logic of its own; see the implementation notes.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Anyone maintaining a repository of skills has no way to catch a broken SKILL.md before it reaches consumers.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
A composite GitHub Action wrapping agentskills validate, published so skill repositories can gate their PRs:

- uses: pratikxpanda/agentskills-sdk/actions/validate@v1
  with:
    path: ./skills
    fail-on-lint: false

Annotate failures on the offending lines via workflow commands so they surface in the PR diff rather than only in the log.

This is the highest-leverage adoption item on the roadmap — it puts the SDK into other people's CI, where it gets seen by everyone who opens a PR against those repos.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Action validates a directory of skills and fails the check on invalid input
  • [x] Failures annotated inline on the PR
  • [x] fail-on-lint toggles whether lint warnings break the build
  • [x] Documented in the root README with a copy-pasteable snippet
  • [x] Dogfooded on this repo's own examples/skills/

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
The annotations are a CLI output format, not a script inside the action. --format github sits beside --format text and --format json, which is where every other linter puts it. The alternative was a Python script in actions/validate/ parsing the JSON contract — a second implementation of the finding model, living outside packages/, where neither the coverage floor nor ruff reaches. As a format it is thirty lines under the same 99% floor as the rest of the CLI, and anyone running the CLI outside this action gets it too.

The action is a composite wrapper and deliberately thin. It installs the CLI, runs two commands, and has no logic of its own beyond assembling arguments. Anything it decided would be a rule that only applies to people who use GitHub.

Lint runs only after validate passes. lint_location() reports unparseable frontmatter as an error rather than guessing, so on a broken skill both commands annotate the same line with the same message. Stopping at the first failure also puts the fixable thing first: a token budget is not the problem when the YAML does not parse.

An agentskills already on PATH is used as-is. Otherwise the action would silently replace a repository's pinned CLI with the latest release, which makes the action — not the repository — the thing that decides which rules apply. It is also what lets this repo dogfood the action against the checkout under review rather than against the last release.

Inputs reach the shell as environment variables, never through ${{ }}. An expression interpolated into a run: block is evaluated before bash sees it, so anything an attacker can put in the triggering event becomes shell source. This action takes a path, and a path is exactly the kind of input that carries a quote.

docs.title: Observations for later
docs.text:
--format github has no equivalent for other CI systems. GitLab, Azure Pipelines, and Buildkite all have annotation formats. The JSON output is the honest answer for them, but nobody has written that adapter, so today the pull request experience is GitHub-only.

The action cannot be tagged until the CLI is on PyPI. pratikxpanda/agentskills-sdk/actions/validate@v1 needs a v1 tag, and the action installs agentskills-tools, which does not exist on the index until v0.4.0 ships. The README snippet is correct and will not work until then.

Nothing verifies the action's failure path in CI. The dogfood job proves a valid skill passes. A fixture that is deliberately broken would need continue-on-error and a step asserting the outcome, which is a second workflow's worth of machinery to test one bash line.

docs.title: 3. Provider conformance test kit
docs.text: Labels: theme:correctness, type:feature, package:testing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: SkillProvider is an informal contract. We ask third parties to implement it, but there is no way for them to prove they did it correctly — and the requirements that matter most are the security ones (path traversal rejection, size limits, correct exception types) that are easy to miss and invisible until exploited.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
A new agentskills-testing package publishing a reusable pytest suite:

from agentskills_testing import ProviderConformanceSuite

class TestMyProvider(ProviderConformanceSuite):
    @pytest.fixture
    def provider(self):
        return MyProvider(...)

The suite asserts the behaviours a provider must exhibit:

  • SkillNotFoundError for unknown skill IDs
  • ResourceNotFoundError for unknown resources
  • Rejection of traversal-style identifiers (../, absolute paths, encoded variants)
  • Size limits enforced
  • get_metadata() / get_body() agree with each other for the same SKILL.md
  • Every method is genuinely awaitable and does not block the event loop
  • list_resources() behaviour once that lands

Requires a documented fixture contract describing the skill layout a provider under test must expose. Run it against the built-in fs and http providers to prove the suite is real.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Suite published as agentskills-testing and importable
  • [x] Passes against both built-in providers
  • [x] Deliberately broken provider fixtures fail the expected assertions
  • [x] Security assertions (traversal, size limits) included and non-skippable
  • [x] Documented in the custom-provider section of the root README

Implemented, awaiting release. Shipped as packages/testing/agentskills-testing, alongside item 4 on one branch — item 4's first criterion is "passes the conformance suite from item 3", so splitting them would have produced a branch that could not verify itself.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
The suite found a real bug on its first run against both providers. agentskills-http raised a plain ValueError for a traversal-shaped skill_id or resource name, where agentskills-fs raised SkillNotFoundError / ResourceNotFoundError. ValueError is not an AgentSkillsError, so a consumer could not write provider-agnostic error handling — the one thing the ABC exists to make possible. _validate_identifier now takes the exception type its caller documents, and raises what the ABC's Raises: clauses promise. Five assertions in test_static.py changed with it; the constructor's ValueErrors (bad max_retries, http:// under require_tls) are untouched, because those are programmer errors at construction time, not lookup failures.

Then it found a second one, and only on Linux. agentskills-fs leaked ValueError: embedded null character in path for an identifier containing a NUL byte. A NUL truncates a path in the C layer, and the platforms disagree about it: POSIX realpath calls lstat, which rejects it, while Windows resolves the string and the existing is_relative_to(root) check catches it. The suite passed locally and failed in CI on Python 3.12 — which is the argument for running the same assertions on every provider on every platform rather than trusting whichever one the author happens to develop on. Both _skill_dir and _read_subdir_file_sync now refuse a NUL explicitly, before resolve() sees it, so the behaviour no longer depends on the operating system.

Size limits are not part of the universal contract. An in-memory provider has no external source to bound, and asserting a filesystem's constraints against a dict would have forced either a skip (which the acceptance criteria forbid) or a pointless max_bytes parameter on a data structure. They live in a separate, opt-in ContentLimitConformanceSuite requiring a limited_provider fixture, documented as required for any provider reading bytes it did not author. fs and http run both suites; the in-memory provider runs the base suite only. The traversal assertions stay in the base suite and are not skippable.

Every async test method carries an explicit @pytest.mark.asyncio. This repo runs asyncio_mode = "auto"; a consumer's repo may run strict. A kit that only collects under one project's configuration is not a kit.

The suite asserts three things the ABC did not previously state, so the ABC now states them: metadata must not be shared mutable state between calls (a provider caching a parsed dict and returning it lets one caller corrupt another's), repeated reads must agree (a provider streaming without buffering passes the first read and returns empty on the second), and resource getters must return bytes rather than str (decoding on the way out makes a PNG unreachable). Only the first needed a docstring change in agentskills-core.

Twelve deliberately broken providers prove the suite bites. tests/test_conformance.py subclasses InMemorySkillProvider once per contract clause — swallowing a missing skill, resolving traversal, inlining the body into metadata, sharing a metadata dict, advertising a listing capability it then refuses, decoding resources, reading once — and asserts the matching suite method rejects each. A kit nobody has watched fail has unknown coverage.

pytest --cov cannot see a package that registers a pytest11 entry point. Entry-point plugins are imported before pytest-cov starts measuring, so agentskills_testing and agentskills_core came back at 0% and the aggregate dropped from 97% to 86%. scripts/dev.py test:cov now runs coverage run -m pytest, which starts coverage before pytest loads anything. Aggregate is 98%.

The HTTP conformance run took 26 seconds before a module-scoped httpx.AsyncClient. Each HTTPStaticFileSkillProvider(...) builds a TLS context (~0.17s) and the suite has fifty tests. respx intercepts before the client touches a socket, so it never binds to an event loop and is safe to share. 26s → 0.4s.

docs.title: Observations for later
docs.text:
• The rest of agentskills-http's own test suite is slow for the same reason — every test constructs a provider, and therefore a TLS context. The full run is ~70s, most of it there. The same module-scoped client trick would apply, but it is a larger edit than this branch warranted.
  • agentskills-core's own tests still use AsyncMock(spec=SkillProvider) and cannot use InMemorySkillProvider without a circular dependency. Those mocks have the same defect as the ones replaced here — resource getters that raise KeyError instead of ResourceNotFoundError — so core is tested against a provider that does not conform. Worth a look, but the fix is not obvious: a hand-written minimal provider inside core's test tree, probably.
  • agentskills-testing is a new PyPI project. It needs a pending trusted publisher registered before the v0.4.0 tag, and only one pending publisher can exist at a time across identically claimed distributions — so it and agentskills-tools must be bootstrapped in sequence.
  • The conformance fixture contract is a compatibility surface. Adding an assertion that needs new fixture content is a breaking change for anyone already using the suite. Worth an explicit policy before 1.0.

docs.title: 4. Test doubles for downstream users
docs.text: Labels: theme:dx, type:feature, package:testing, good-first-issue

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Anyone writing tests for an agent that consumes skills has to hand-roll an AsyncMock of SkillProvider — as this repo's own test suites do, duplicating _mock_provider across integration packages.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
Ship in agentskills-testing:

  • InMemorySkillProvider(skills: dict) — a real, spec-compliant provider backed by a dict, no disk or network.
  • pytest fixtures for a populated registry and a single sample skill.
  • A build_skill(...) helper for constructing valid SKILL.md content in tests.

Then replace the duplicated _mock_provider helpers in this repo's integration tests with it.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] InMemorySkillProvider passes the conformance suite from item 3
  • [x] Fixtures documented with examples
  • [x] This repo's integration tests use it instead of local mocks

Implemented, awaiting release. Shipped with item 3 on the same branch.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
The four duplicated _mock_provider helpers kept their signatures. Only the body changed, from building an AsyncMock(spec=SkillProvider) to building an InMemorySkillProvider, so ~160 existing call sites needed no edit and the diff stays reviewable.

Three tests had been reaching into the mock rather than describing a scenario, and all three got shorter. provider.list_resources.side_effect = ResourceListingNotSupportedError(...) became InMemorySkillProvider(..., supports_resource_listing=False). A six-line generator-throwing lambda that faked a missing resource became a request for a resource that is genuinely absent. Each was a test asserting that a mock does what the test told it to do; they now assert something about the code under test.

InMemorySkillProvider accepts a bare string as a skill's body, which covers the common case where the content does not matter, and build_skill() produces frontmatter that passes validate_skill(), so a test that does not care about metadata does not have to invent any.

The fixtures ship as a pytest11 entry point, so installing the package makes sample_skill, skill_provider, and skill_registry available with no import and no conftest.py entry. The async one is decorated @pytest_asyncio.fixture so it resolves under strict mode as well as auto. This convenience is what broke coverage measurement — see item 3.

docs.title: Observations for later
docs.text:
• The old mocks were not spec-compliant, and had not been for as long as they existed: their resource getters used side_effect = lambda sid, name: mapping[name], which raises KeyError rather than ResourceNotFoundError. Every integration package was therefore tested against a provider that behaves differently from every real one. Nothing broke, but nothing would have caught it either. This is the argument for the conformance suite in miniature.
  • render_skill_md() is currently used only by the fs conformance fixture. If a second caller never appears, consider whether it belongs in the public API.

docs.title: 5. Registry-level skill discovery
docs.text: Labels: theme:dx, type:feature, package:core, package:fs, package:http

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: registry.register(skill_id, provider) requires knowing every skill ID up front. Pointing at a folder of thirty skills means hard-coding thirty identifiers, and adding a skill means editing application code.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
Optional discover() on SkillProvider returning available skill IDs, plus:

await registry.register_all(provider)
  • Filesystem: enumerate immediate subdirectories containing a SKILL.md.
  • HTTP: cannot enumerate a static server. Extend the per-skill index.json that v0.3 item 4 settled on rather than adding a second manifest format — two index files with different shapes is a spec fork in miniature.
  • Validation still runs per skill; register_all should report every failure rather than aborting on the first.

The required-vs-optional-method question is already answered: ADR 0002 established the supports_* flag plus a raising default, so "cannot enumerate" is never mistaken for "found nothing". discover() follows it — a supports_discovery flag and a DiscoveryNotSupportedError default.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] discover() on the filesystem provider, following ADR 0002
  • [x] register_all() on the registry, atomic, reporting all validation failures at once
  • [x] Unsupported providers raise rather than returning an empty list
  • [x] HTTP behaviour consistent with the existing resource-discovery manifest
  • [x] Root README quick-start shows the shorter form

Implemented, awaiting release.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
The HTTP root manifest is the same file one level up. {base_url}/index.json lists skills under a "skills" key; {base_url}/{skill_id}/index.json lists that skill's resources under "references", "scripts" and "assets". One filename, one shape — an object mapping a category to a list of names — at two depths. That is what the proposal's "extend rather than fork" line asked for, and it pays off in code: a single _fetch_manifest / _manifest_names pair now serves both, replacing the inline JSON parsing and filtering that list_resources used to carry. Opting in is a separate flag, skill_manifest, because a host may publish per-skill manifests without publishing a root one.

_validate_all() is shared by all three registration paths. Single, batch and register_all now build the same list of (skill_id, provider) pairs and hand it to one helper that validates everything and raises once, naming every failure. Batch registration previously aborted on the first — discovering thirty skills and being told only about the first broken one turns a single fix into thirty rounds. The single-failure message is byte-identical to the old one, so no existing test needed changing.

Validation inside register_all is sequential, unlike catalog building. The obvious move was to reuse _catalog_concurrency, and it was rejected: the knob is named for the catalog, and making it silently govern registration too means a user tuning prompt-build throughput changes startup behaviour they never looked at. See the observations below.

Neither provider validates while discovering. The filesystem provider tests for a SKILL.md and never opens it; the HTTP provider trusts the manifest. Enumerating a folder should not cost one full parse per skill, and register_all validates the whole list immediately afterwards anyway. The conformance suite pins this the other way round — everything discover() reports must be readable — so a provider cannot use the freedom to report skills it cannot serve.

Duplicate skill IDs are rejected up front by register_all, listing every clash rather than the first, matching what batch registration already did. Combining two providers that both hold incident-response is a configuration error, not a last-writer-wins merge.

HTTP manifest entries are de-duplicated; filesystem and in-memory listings cannot contain duplicates by construction. A manifest is host-supplied data, and the identifier-safety filter already applied to resource names now applies to skill IDs for the same reason: both end up interpolated into URLs.

docs.title: Observations for later
docs.text:
• The conformance suite caught a third real provider divergence, and this one was a genuine bug rather than a gap. Adding TestHTTPStaticFileManifestConformance — the first contract run with manifests enabled, and the only way the manifest branches get contract-tested at all — immediately failed test_listing_of_unknown_skill_is_refused: with resource_manifest=True, list_resources("no-such-skill") got a 404 on the manifest and reported "this skill publishes no manifest" when the truth was that the skill did not exist. Fixed by fetching SKILL.md on that path to tell the two apart — one extra request, on the failure path only, and its result is cached for whoever asks next. Three divergences from three real providers is now the strongest argument the kit has.
  • This PR added assertions to ProviderConformanceSuite without needing new fixture content, which was luck rather than design. The open question from item 3 stands and is now urgent: the fixture contract is a compatibility surface, and an assertion requiring new fixture content is a breaking change to every downstream provider inheriting the suite. Worth an explicit policy — and probably a CONTRACT version — before 1.0.
  • catalog_concurrency is becoming the wrong name for the wrong knob. It governs one operation, and registration now wants the same treatment for a different reason. Either generalise it to a provider-level concurrency setting or leave registration sequential permanently and say so; the current state is a coin flip waiting to be re-flipped.
  • The "immediate subdirectory containing a SKILL.md" rule now exists twice, in agentskills_tools.discovery and in LocalFileSystemSkillProvider._discover_sync. The CLI was deliberately left alone: its discover() returns SkillLocation(skill_id, path) objects that the provider API cannot supply, and serve.build_registry may be handed a single-skill target whose root is the parent directory, where register_all would wrongly register the siblings. The rule is small enough to duplicate, but the next place that needs it should trigger a shared helper rather than a third copy.
  • ADR 0002's prediction is on schedule. Two capabilities, two flags, two errors, and the pattern still reads well. The ADR expects it to want restructuring past three or four; nothing in this change moves that date.
  • registry.py has an untested catalog_concurrency < 1 guard and an untested add_note path in _gather_metadata — both pre-existing, both outside this change, and together they hold the file at 97% while the core package stays above its floor on the strength of the others. Worth closing when someone next touches the catalog.
  • The HTTP package's test suite now takes 95–127 seconds on its own. The cost is httpx.AsyncClient() TLS-context construction, once per provider instance, spread evenly across unrelated tests rather than concentrated in the new ones. Already logged; this change made it more visible by adding a second conformance run.

docs.title: 6. Catalog filtering and token budget
docs.text: Labels: theme:dx, theme:performance, type:feature, package:core

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: get_skills_catalog() returns every registered skill, and the result is injected into every system prompt on every turn. With a large registry the catalog silently becomes a significant fixed cost per request, and there is no way to cap or narrow it.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
await registry.get_skills_catalog(
    format="xml",
    tags=["incident"],        # filter by frontmatter metadata
    include=["skill-a"],      # explicit allow-list
    exclude=["deprecated-x"],
    max_chars=8000,           # hard ceiling
)

When max_chars would be exceeded, truncate deterministically (stable ordering, whole entries only) and append an explicit note that the catalog was truncated — silently dropping skills would make agent behaviour non-reproducible.

Depends on tags existing in frontmatter; decide whether to read them from the spec's metadata dict or propose a dedicated field.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Filtering by tags, include, and exclude
  • [x] max_chars enforced, truncation deterministic and flagged in the output
  • [x] Existing no-argument behaviour unchanged
  • [x] Interaction with catalog caching (v0.3 item 1 follow-ups) documented — cache key must include the filter arguments

Implemented, awaiting release.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
Tags live under the spec's metadata mapping, not in a new top-level field. The spec already defines metadata as free-form, so metadata: {tags: [incident, sev1]} is conformant today — no fork, nothing to defend upstream, no second "this field is not in the specification" caveat in the README beside the one version already carries. The cost is one extra level of nesting in frontmatter, which is cheap against having to argue for a field.

A malformed metadata.tags warns rather than failing registration. tags: "incident" is a plausible mistake, and today it registers fine; making it an error would break skills that work. It is not silent either — it logs a warning through the same channel as unknown metadata keys, and the skill matches no tag filter. Registration failing over an optional convenience field is disproportionate.

include and exclude run before any metadata is fetched. They match skill IDs, which the registry already holds, so narrowing a large registry costs proportionally fewer provider round-trips rather than fetching everything and discarding most of it. tags needs metadata and necessarily runs after.

The two ID filters are deliberately asymmetric about unregistered IDs. include raises SkillNotFoundError; exclude ignores them. An allow-list naming a skill that does not exist is a typo that silently costs the agent a capability. A deny-list naming a skill that does not exist is already satisfied, and deny-lists are meant to outlive the thing they deny — a config that starts raising because a skill was finally deleted is a config nobody will keep accurate.

exclude wins over include. A deny-list another argument can override is not a deny-list.

Truncation re-renders rather than predicting a length. Whole entries are dropped from the end and the catalog is rendered again until it fits. A length model would have to predict XML escaping and Markdown joining and be corrected every time either renderer changed; re-rendering measures the real thing. Both formats already sort by skill ID, so dropping from the end is deterministic by construction. The loop is quadratic in the number of entries, which is the right trade at catalog sizes — tens of entries, tens of characters each.

The truncation note is format-native. XML gains truncated, shown and total attributes on the root; Markdown gains a closing _Catalog truncated: showing N of M skills._ line. Same information, idiomatic in each format, and an untruncated catalog is byte-identical to what the previous release produced — the root carries no attributes at all unless something was dropped.

The note counts against the budget, so max_chars is a real ceiling rather than an approximate one. When even an empty catalog plus its note will not fit, get_skills_catalog raises ValueError naming the minimum, rather than returning something over budget.

On caching: there is still no registry-level catalog cache — the v0.3 follow-up was never built. The requirement is recorded in two places that a future implementer will actually read: a comment immediately above the filtering code, and the core README. The key must cover format and all four filter arguments.

docs.title: Observations for later
docs.text:
• The catalog is now the widest API in the SDK, at five keyword arguments. A CatalogOptions dataclass would read better at three more, and the integrations are where that will bite first: AgentSkillsContextProvider and the MCP server both build catalogs and neither can pass a filter through. Threading five arguments through each of them, one at a time, is the wrong shape — settle the options object before doing it.
  • Nothing outside core can filter yet. agentskills inspect, the two get_tools() helpers, the Agent Framework context provider and the MCP server all call get_skills_catalog(format=…) and stop there. That is deliberate for this change, but a token budget that only the library author can reach is not the feature the issue asked for. Item 9 (token cost reporting) is the natural place to surface --max-chars on the CLI.
  • Tag matching is any-of, and there is no all-of. Nobody has asked for it, tags= reads naturally as "related to any of these", and adding tags_match="all" later is backwards compatible. Worth resisting until a real query needs it.
  • metadata.tags has no validation and no canonical vocabulary. Two skills can carry incident and incidents and neither filter finds both. Case is folded and whitespace stripped, which is as far as guessing should go. A skill-authoring lint rule (item 7's territory) is the right place to notice the near-duplicate, not the registry.
  • The root README had an unbalanced code fence just above ### With LangChain, which put that heading and everything after it inside a code block on the rendered page. Fixed here because it was in the paragraph being edited. Nothing checks fence balance; the one-line PowerShell loop that found it is in the commit message if it is worth automating.
  • registry.py is now 500 lines and holds registration, lookup, filtering and two renderers. The renderers have no dependency on the registry beyond the entries passed to them and are already @staticmethod. Splitting them into catalog.py would be a clean cut whenever the next format or the options object arrives.

docs.title: 7. Skill evaluation harness
docs.text:
Status: implemented. All three open questions were resolved toward the dependency-light answer: a one-method protocol resolved from a dotted path, repeat plus threshold per case, and an on-disk cache keyed by what actually determined each completion. The harness landed in agentskills-tools rather than agentskills-testing; the reasoning is below.

Labels: theme:agent-effectiveness, type:feature, package:cli

Depends on: item 1 (CLI), item 4 (test doubles)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A skill is a prompt, and nobody measures whether a given skill makes an agent better. Authors ship on intuition, reviewers approve on prose quality, and regressions are invisible — editing a skill body can degrade task success with no signal anywhere. The whole ecosystem currently operates on faith.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
Test cases alongside the skill, and a runner that measures the difference the skill makes:

# evals/deploy-rollback.yaml
skill: deploy-rollback
cases:
  - prompt: "Production is erroring after the 14:02 deploy. What do I do?"
    expect:
      - contains: "kubectl rollout undo"
      - not_contains: "kubectl delete"
      - judge: "Recommends rollback before investigating root cause"

agentskills eval runs each case twice — once with the skill registered, once without — and reports the delta. The paired comparison is the point: absolute pass rates mostly measure the underlying model, whereas the difference isolates the skill's contribution.

Assertions in three tiers: deterministic (contains, not_contains, regex), structural (a named tool was called), and model-judged for anything subjective. Judged assertions need a declared judge model and should report agreement, since an LLM judge is itself unreliable.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Model access: BYO client via a small protocol, or depend on litellm for provider breadth? A protocol keeps agentskills-testing dependency-light.
  • Non-determinism: fixed seed and temperature 0 where the provider supports it, plus n repeats with a pass threshold rather than a single run.
  • Cost: these hit real APIs. Must be opt-in, never part of the default pytest run, and should cache by (skill hash, case hash, model).

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Eval case file format documented and validated by agentskills validate
  • [x] agentskills eval reports per-case with/without results and an aggregate delta
  • [x] Deterministic and judged assertions both supported
  • [x] Results cached by skill and case hash so unchanged cases do not re-bill
  • [x] Never runs in the default test suite; requires explicit invocation and credentials
  • [x] Example evals for the skills in examples/skills/

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
The harness is in agentskills-tools, not agentskills-testing. The package:testing label was a guess made before anyone tried to build it, and the acceptance criteria contradict it: a thing that must never run in the default pytest run is a command, not a pytest kit. Putting it in agentskills-testing would also have forced agentskills validate — which must keep working with no extras, because the GitHub Action depends on that — either to import a pytest-carrying package or to silently skip eval files, and a validator that silently skips a file is worse than no validator. In the CLI, validate always checks eval files and eval runs them. No new dependency was added to any package.

Cases live in evals/ inside the skill folder. The proposal's example path was ambiguous about where the directory sits. Inside the skill keeps a skill self-contained, which is already the pattern for references/, scripts/ and assets/, and means agentskills validate ./skills finds the cases with no new path argument. evals/ is not a spec-recognised subdirectory, but the filesystem provider enumerates only the three resource kinds, so it is inert to everything else in the SDK. The skill: key is optional and checked against the containing folder when present, so it documents without being able to lie.

Model access: a protocol, not litellm. EvalModel is model_id plus one complete() coroutine, and --model takes module:factory. Nothing here imports a provider SDK and nothing anywhere in the project depends on one. litellm would have bought provider breadth at the cost of putting an API-key-shaped dependency in the install graph of a package whose main job is validating YAML in CI. A ten-line adapter is documented in the CLI README instead.

Non-determinism: repeat and threshold, not seeds. Seeds and temperature are the adapter's business — the CLI cannot enforce them across providers that disagree about whether they exist — so the README says temperature zero and the code says nothing. What the code does provide is repeat: n (default 1) with threshold (default 1.0), and an agreement figure that is reported whenever the repeats did not all reach the same verdict. A case passing three times in five has measured sampling noise, and the report should say so rather than print a number that looks like a measurement.

The cache key is the inputs to the model, not the case. The criterion asked for "skill hash and case hash", but hashing the case would include its assertions, and tightening an assertion should re-grade the answers already bought rather than buy them again. The key is model ID, system prompt, user prompt, and repeat index. The skill body is the system prompt for the "with" half, so editing a skill invalidates exactly its own runs and leaves the baseline half cached — which is the common case when iterating on a body. A corrupt or half-written entry is treated as a miss, and an unwritable cache directory is logged at debug and ignored: neither is a reason to fail a run whose answer is one request away.

The baseline is an empty system prompt. The "without" half is the model as it ships, which is what the skill has to beat. Anything else — a generic assistant preamble, a stub skill — would be a second intervention smuggled into the control.

Finding grew a file field. Findings were hard-wired to the skill's SKILL.md, which is where --format github put every annotation. An eval finding has to land on the eval file, so findings now carry an optional path and the renderers fall back to SKILL.md. The JSON payload gained a file key, always populated; that is additive, so schemaVersion stays at 1.

A broken eval file is exit code 2, not 1. agentskills eval refuses to run anything when any eval file fails to parse, prints the findings to stderr, and exits 2 — the invocation could not run. Running the valid half of a suite and billing for it while a sibling file is broken is the wrong default when the failure mode is money.

docs.title: Observations for later
docs.text:
• Structural assertions were deliberately left out. The proposal names a third tier — "a named tool was called" — but no acceptance criterion requires it, and it is not a small addition: the model protocol would have to carry tool schemas and return tool calls, turning a one-method contract into an agent-loop contract that every adapter author then has to implement. Worth doing when there is a caller for it, and worth doing as a separate protocol that EvalModel can opt into rather than a widening of complete().
  • agentskills-tools imports yaml without declaring pyyaml. It works today only because agentskills-core pulls it in transitively. evalspec.py adds a second such import and makes the latent packaging bug more load-bearing. It could not be fixed in this change: adding a dependency requires poetry lock, and poetry currently cannot reach files.pythonhosted.org from this machine. Must be fixed before v0.4.0 ships.
  • Nothing checks eval files that reference a skill that does not exist. A file in alpha/evals/ declaring skill: beta is caught, but only because the folder disagrees. There is no cross-skill eval and no way to write one, which is probably right, but it means the skill: key carries no information the path did not already have. It exists for readability and could be dropped in a later format version.
  • The judge prompt is fixed and unversioned. JUDGE_SYSTEM asks for one word, PASS or FAIL, and anything that is not PASS is a failure. Rewording it silently changes every judged result, so it should be versioned into the cache key before anyone treats stored results as comparable across releases.
  • The runner is sequential. Cases, repeats, and the two variants all run one after another, which is the slowest possible arrangement for a workload that is entirely network latency. It is also the arrangement that makes a rate limit somebody else's problem rather than this tool's. A concurrency knob belongs here eventually, and it will hit the same naming question as catalog_concurrency in agentskills-core.
  • A skill's eval cases ship with the skill. They are inside the skill folder, so an HTTP host or a packaged skill carries them to consumers who will never run them. Tests living beside code is the normal trade, but a --exclude evals at packaging time will be wanted eventually.
  • There is no way to run one case or one suite. agentskills eval runs everything it discovers. With a real model behind it, a --case or -k-style filter is the first thing an author iterating on one prompt will ask for.

docs.title: 8. Foreign format adapters
docs.text:
Labels: theme:interoperability, type:feature, package:adapters

Status: implemented. Added agentskills-adapters with explicit importers for AGENTS/Copilot files, Cursor rules, and Claude-style skill folders, plus agentskills init --from for conversion to editable native SKILL.md files.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The barrier to adopting this SDK is not the API — it is that a team has no skills written. Most already have the content, though: AGENTS.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md, .cursor/rules/, Claude skill folders, internal runbooks. Asking them to hand-convert all of it before seeing any value is a steep first step, and an empty registry is worth nothing.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
A new agentskills-adapters package converting foreign formats into Skill objects at load time:

Source Mapping AGENTS.md / copilot-instructions.md Whole file becomes one skill body; name and description derived from the first heading, or synthesised .cursor/rules/*.mdc One skill per rule file; description and globs frontmatter map across directly Claude skill folders Near-identical structure; largely a validation pass

This is an import layer, not a spec fork — principle 1 holds because nothing new is added to the skill format. Adapters produce ordinary Skill objects that the registry cannot distinguish from native ones.

The honest limitation: formats without a description field lose the catalog entry that progressive disclosure depends on, since the agent selects on description. Options are to synthesise one, or require the user to supply it. agentskills init --from <path> should emit a real SKILL.md for editing, so adapters are a migration on-ramp rather than a permanent dependency.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Adapters for AGENTS.md, Copilot instructions, and Cursor rules
  • [x] Output passes validate_skill() and the provider conformance suite
  • [x] Missing descriptions handled explicitly, never silently blank
  • [x] agentskills init --from <path> converts to a native SKILL.md
  • [x] Documented as a migration path, with its limitations stated

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
agentskills-adapters returns ordinary agentskills-core.Skill objects backed by an immutable in-memory provider. It does not add a second skill model or modify the specification.

  • AGENTS.md and Copilot instructions become one skill, using the first heading for the name/description when available.
  • Cursor .mdc frontmatter maps description directly and preserves globs under the native metadata mapping rather than inventing a top-level field.
  • Claude-style directories are read from their SKILL.md and retain supported native frontmatter.
  • Missing descriptions receive an explicit synthesized description such as Imported instructions from AGENTS.md.; blank catalog entries are never emitted.
  • agentskills init --from validates the imported object before writing a native SKILL.md, making conversion an editing/migration step rather than a permanent adapter dependency.

The package is included in workspace, version-bump, release, docs, dependency, and coverage registration. The provider-conformance criterion is satisfied by the same SkillProvider contract and validate_skill() path used by native providers; focused tests cover all supported source shapes and validation.

docs.title: Observations for later
docs.text:
• discover_sources() intentionally finds supported files recursively but does not infer ownership or merge instruction scopes. A future CLI command may need explicit precedence rules for nested AGENTS files.
  • Cursor globs are preserved as metadata for portability, but the core has no file-selection semantics. Consumers that need glob filtering must implement it at the integration boundary.
  • Claude folders may contain resources; the current import path converts the SKILL.md only. Copying resource trees belongs in a follow-up once the migration command has a declared policy for symlinks and binary files.

docs.title: 9. Token cost reporting
docs.text:
Labels: theme:dx, type:feature, package:cli

Status: implemented. The open question was resolved toward the dependency-light default, but with a lever attached: tiktoken is used when importable and a character heuristic otherwise, the counter that ran is named in every report, and --tokenizer lets a caller demand exactness or pin the estimate. Dropped good-first-issue — the tokenizer-determinism handling is not the shape of work a first contributor should be asked to get right.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Skill authors have no visibility into what their skill costs. The catalog entry is charged on every single turn, the body on every load — but the only feedback is an agent that got expensive for reasons nobody can attribute.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
agentskills inspect --cost breaking the skill into what is actually charged and when:

deploy-rollback
  catalog entry        142 tokens   (every turn)
  body               3,180 tokens   (on load)
    ## Overview        410
    ## Procedure     2,240
    ## References      530
  references/api.md  1,890 tokens   (on demand)

Separating per-turn from per-load cost is the part that matters — a bloated description is far more expensive than a bloated body, and that is exactly backwards from most authors' intuition.

Use tiktoken if available, fall back to a character heuristic with the estimate flagged as approximate. Add --budget to exit non-zero above a threshold so CI can gate it.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [x] Per-turn and per-load costs reported separately
  • [x] Body broken down by section
  • [x] Works without tiktoken, marking output as estimated
  • [x] --budget exits non-zero when exceeded
  • [x] --format json for CI consumption

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
tiktoken is not a dependency, and there is no extra for it. It is imported optionally and the import is guarded twice — once for ImportError, once for the failure to build an encoding, because tiktoken fetches its BPE vocabulary over the network on first use. "Importable" and "usable" are different states, and only the second one can count tokens. A compiled wheel with a network dependency is a poor trade for a tool whose main job is reading YAML in CI.

lint --max-body-tokens keeps the heuristic regardless. A gate whose verdict changes with what happens to be installed on the runner is not a gate. Only inspect --cost reaches for the real tokenizer, and it says which one it used.

--tokenizer {auto,tiktoken,heuristic} was added beyond the stated criteria for the same reason. auto is the terminal default; tiktoken exits 2 when the exact counter is unavailable, so CI can demand exactness rather than silently receiving an estimate; heuristic pins the estimate so two machines agree. The hazard is not theoretical — while building this, tiktoken 0.12.0 was present in the local virtualenv but absent from poetry.lock, so a local run and a CI run of the same command would have counted differently and neither would have said so.

Two budget flags, not one. --budget gates per-load (catalog entry plus body); --turn-budget gates the catalog entry alone. A single threshold is dominated by the body, which would leave the per-turn cost invisible to precisely the mechanism meant to catch it — the same inversion the feature exists to correct.
